activities.anchor: learned in an ordered ladder of instruments
activities.caption: rebuild the instrument ladder, coarsest first
activities.name: machLadderOrder

config.prompt: Rebuild the metrology ladder in order of resolution:
items: steel rule — readable to roughly 0.5 mm
vernier caliper — inside, outside, depth and step to about 0.02 mm, the daily workhorse
micrometer — 0.01 mm with a vernier, 0.001 mm digital or fine
dial indicator — 0.01 mm per division, turning "is it straight?" into a number
gauge blocks — lapped so flat they wring together, the shop's physical truth
CMM — probes features in three axes for the highest-accuracy inspection
config.why: Choose an instrument whose resolution is finer than a tenth of the tolerance — and never trust a measurement whose instrument you have not verified.

activities.anchor: until the procedure behind it is sound
activities.caption: find the line the ritual refutes
activities.name: machRitualSpot

config.prompt: One line of this metrology report is wrong — click it:
lines: A micrometer's number is evidence about the part, not the part itself.
A dirty anvil can move a "precise" number by more than the tolerance you are judging.
A part measured ten degrees warm reads exactly the same as at reference temperature.
The ritual is clean, zero-check, measure with consistent force, repeat, record.
Professionals are suspicious of any measurement taken too quickly to be doubted.
config.correction: Steel expands about 11.7 µm per metre per °C — a warm part can pass and fail cold, which is why precision shops soak parts and gauges at 20 °C.
config.why: The micrometer itself grows with your hand — one more reason measurement is a procedure, not a gesture.

activities.anchor: Above the hand tools sits the reference hierarchy
activities.caption: pair each instrument with its job
activities.name: machRefMatch

config.prompt: The reference hierarchy — pair each instrument with what it does:

pairs.right: the shop's physical truth — hardened blocks lapped so flat they wring together, traceable to national standards
granite flat to microns — the datum plane from which height gauges and scribes work
runout, alignment and deflection — "is it straight?" becomes a number
go/no-go verdicts faster than any reading
probes features in three axes for the highest-accuracy inspection

config.why: Calibrations trace the blocks back to national standards — metrology's formal chain of traceability.

activities.anchor: tolerance is the economic engine of the trade
activities.caption: true or false — the cost of tight
activities.name: machTolJudge

statements.why: Error sources that vanish at ±0.2 mm dominate at ±0.02 mm.

statements.s: A clearance hole can be ±0.5 mm; a bearing journal needs ±0.01 mm.
Beyond what the function needs, tightness is pure cost — slower processes, more scrap, more inspection.
statements.why: Knowing how tight is tight enough separates a machinist from an operator.

statements.s: A clearance hole made to ±0.01 mm works noticeably better than one at ±0.5 mm.
statements.why: It works exactly the same and costs far more — the tolerance chooses the machine, the tooling, the sequence and the price.

activities.anchor: deliberately offset toward the safe side
activities.caption: bet on where the professional aims
activities.name: machAimPredict

config.q: Tool wear moves dimensions across a production run. Where does a professional aim the first cut?
choices: dead on the exact nominal number
external dimensions slightly over nominal, holes slightly under — leaving room for wear and finishing
at the limit that passes most parts
wherever the first part happens to land
config.why: Targeting the middle of the band is engineering; targeting the nominal is hope — aim so tool wear and finishing have room to work without crossing a limit.

activities.anchor: The physics underneath all of it is a triangle
activities.caption: call the surface speed stainless can take
activities.name: machSpeedEstimate

config.prompt: Cutting-data tables give each alloy a workable envelope. Roughly what surface speed does 304 stainless with a carbide cutter tolerate?
config.why: Around 40 m/min — versus roughly 250 for 6061 aluminium with the same 12 mm carbide end mill: more than a sixfold difference, and stainless wants a heavier per-tooth feed to stay under the work-hardened surface.
config.context: Speed drives heat; feed and depth drive cutting force — the heat that should leave in the chip is what cooks a titanium or stainless edge.

activities.caption: walk three cuts that fight back
activities.name: machAlloyBranch

config.root: Each alloy teaches a different lesson at the cut — walk two of them.

start.text: Material: 304 stainless. Mid-pass, your tool starts dwelling and rubbing instead of cutting. What now?

choices.label: Speed up to power through
choices.feedback: More heat into the same surface.

choices.label: Constant feed, sharp tools, adequate depth of cut

worse.text: Dwell work-hardens the surface under the tool — the next pass now cuts harder material than the drawing's alloy. Hardness is not the villain; the work-hardening plus heat is.

choices.label: Reset with the countermeasures and continue to titanium

fix1.text: Constant feed and adequate depth keep the cutter always under fresh metal — the countermeasures for work-hardening.

titanium.text: Material: titanium. The cutting edge is cooking. Why?

choices.label: Terrible thermal conductivity — the heat cannot leave in the chip
Titanium is simply too hard for carbide

ti-ok.text: High strength, low elasticity (it springs away and rubs) and heat trapped at the edge — hence low speeds, flood coolant and rigid setups.

ti-wrong.text: Hardness is not the villain here either — the problem is heat that cannot leave in the chip: low speeds, flood coolant, rigid setups.

config.why: Brass and bronze machine freely — which is why they are the traditional apprentice metals.
